title: How Thanksgiving Really Became a Holiday (It Took 320 Years)
description:
Everyone knows the Pilgrim story. But the holiday on your table this Thursday took 320 years to build, from a three-day harvest gathering in 1621 to a law Roosevelt signed in 1941.
🚶 Visiting San Diego? Explore its history on a guided tour with Fable: https://fablehospitality.com

Thanksgiving is in the news all week, so here is the full history behind it: what Edward Winslow actually wrote about the 1621 harvest gathering with Ousamequin (the Massasoit) and about ninety Wampanoag men; how New England's days of thanksgiving became a family dinner; why Washington proclaimed November 26, 1789 and Jefferson refused; how editor Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for 17 years until Lincoln's 1863 proclamation; how an 1841 footnote and Bradford's rediscovered manuscript turned 1621 into "the first Thanksgiving"; and how "Franksgiving" split the country in 1939 until Congress fixed the fourth Thursday of November.

Every frame is drawn with code. No stock footage, no AI video.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Cold open: the story we all learned
0:44 Chapter 1: Three days in 1621
2:41 Chapter 2: A holiday with no date
3:50 Chapter 3: The editor who wouldn't quit
5:29 Chapter 4: Inventing the first Thanksgiving
6:47 Chapter 5: Franksgiving
7:59 Payoff: built in layers

A NOTE ON SOURCES
The only eyewitness account of the 1621 gathering is Edward Winslow's letter, printed in "Mourt's Relation" (London, 1622); William Bradford's history adds that there was "great store of wild turkeys" that fall. Whether turkey was served at the 1621 meal isn't recorded, so the video says "maybe." Pilgrim Hall Museum dates the alliance with Ousamequin to spring 1621 (Mourt's Relation records the first meeting on March 22, 1621). King Philip's War (1675-76) is described as one of the deadliest wars in colonial America by most historians; casualty estimates vary. The state counts for 1939 (23 states and D.C. on November 23, 22 on November 30, and Colorado, Mississippi and Texas on both) follow the National Archives' Prologue magazine and contemporary newspaper tallies.
